## Status

Discussion document, 2026-09-22. Nothing here is fitted or authorised for a
refit. It answers one question raised in the model review — *can the Whittle
likelihood tell us about slowly wandering amplitudes?* — and then writes down
the model that collects every change agreed in that review, with its fitting
procedure. Every statement about the current model points at the code:
`src/experiments/noise_model/model.py` (parameters and priors,
`class Priors` and `sample_params`), `src/experiments/noise_model/fit.py`

(the renderer). Numbers quoted from fits name their file under

# The short answer

The current model (v2) has **no amplitude wander**: a rendered clip's line
powers and floor shape are fixed by the rig parameters and the rotor-speed
trajectory; only the phases are random
(`render.py`, module docstring). The claim "the Whittle likelihood cannot see
slow wander" is true **of that model** — a constant parameter cannot absorb a
zero-mean fluctuation, so the fluctuation leaves no trace in the fit — and
**false of the model proposed here**, where every block of a few hundred
milliseconds gets its own amplitude latent with a prior centred on the clip's
mean. Each block's periodogram is then fully informative about that block's
amplitude, and the wander's size and memory are the spread and the
autocorrelation of the block latents. It is the floor-spline construction —
a smooth curve with a Gaussian prior — applied along time instead of along
frequency.

The rest of the page is the reasoning at the level of someone who has not met
a periodogram before, then the modified model, then its fit.

# Part 1 — what the likelihood sees

## 1.1 A periodogram cell

Take one microphone, cut the audio into frames of $N = 2048$ samples
(128 ms at 16 kHz), hop 512, window each frame with a Hann taper and take
the Fourier transform. The squared magnitude at frequency bin $f$ of frame
$n$ is one **periodogram cell** $I_m(n, f)$: "how much power was there at
frequency $f$ during frame $n$".

For a Gaussian signal, each cell is a random number whose **mean** is the
signal's power spectral density at that frequency, $S_m(n, f)$, and whose
distribution is exponential:

$$
I_m(n,f) \;\sim\; S_m(n,f)\cdot \mathrm{Exp}(1), \qquad
\mathbb E[I] = S,\quad \operatorname{sd}[I] = S .
$$

So a single cell tells you the local power to within a factor of $e^{\pm 1}$ —
very noisy — and cells at different frequencies (and, for a taper with hop
$\ge N/4$, different frames) are approximately independent.

## 1.2 The Whittle likelihood

Given a model that predicts the density $S_\theta(n, f)$ from parameters
$\theta$, the log-likelihood of all the cells under the exponential law is

$$
\ell(\theta) \;=\; -\sum_{m,n,f}\Big[\log S_\theta(m,n,f) + \frac{I_m(n,f)}{S_\theta(m,n,f)}\Big] .
$$

That is the Whittle likelihood. It is an approximation (it ignores the
correlation between neighbouring cells that the taper introduces) but it is
the standard one for spectral fitting and it is what every v2 fit maximises
(`fit.py`, the objective; the composite variant pools frames of a window that
share a carrier, but the form is the same).

Two properties matter below.

::: {.def}
**(W1) A scale is easy to estimate from many cells.** If $n$ independent
cells share one unknown scale $\theta$ (their model is $S = \theta \cdot
\text{shape}$ with the shape known), the maximum-likelihood estimate is the
mean of the ratios $I/\text{shape}$ and its relative standard deviation is
$1/\sqrt n$. In decibels: $\operatorname{sd} \approx 4.34/\sqrt n$ dB. Ten
cells give $\pm 1.4$ dB, a hundred give $\pm 0.4$ dB.
:::

::: {.def}
**(W2) The likelihood only sees the mean of each cell.** Everything the fit
learns about $\theta$ comes through $S_\theta$. A random effect that changes
the true density from frame to frame but leaves a constant model in place
can only show up as a bias of the constant — not as a separate parameter.
:::

## 1.3 Why the constant-amplitude model is blind

Suppose the true line power at order $k$ of rotor $i$ is not constant but
wanders slowly:

$$
P_{ik}(t) \;=\; \bar P_{ik}\, 10^{d_{ik}(t)/10}, \qquad
d_{ik} \text{ slow, zero-mean, sd } \sigma_d \text{ dB}.
$$

The v2 model has one number $\bar P_{ik}$ (well, $p_{ik} = 10\log_{10}\bar P_{ik}$,
site `profile_db`) for the whole pool. Under (W2), the fit's best constant is
the one whose density matches the cells on average, i.e. roughly the
time-mean of $P_{ik}(t)$, which is $\bar P_{ik}\, e^{(0.23\,\sigma_d)^2/2}$ — a
slight upward bias. That is all. The **variance** of the wander is invisible:
the cells' spread around their mean is already the exponential law's own
spread, and a model with one constant has nowhere to put an extra spread.
Nothing in `Priors` or `sample_params` corresponds to $\sigma_d$.

Whatever the real amplitude variation is, the current fit therefore either
ignores it or pushes it into a parameter that *can* change the per-frame
density: the line width $\gamma_{ik}$ (a line that fades in and out over
frames looks, in a pooled periodogram, like a broader hump than a steady
line) or the per-mic gains. The degenerate widths found in every fit
(`round5/fits/dregon_room2_floor__flight_profile.json`: 7223 Hz at $k=65$;
`round3/fits/michaels_fly125_cruise__flight.json`: 125 578 Hz at $k=18$ on
rotor 3) are consistent with that escape route, though they also have the
prior explanation given in the model review (a log-normal prior is quadratic
in $\log\gamma$ and charges only ~40 nats for a 7 kHz line).

## 1.4 Why per-block latents make it visible

Now give every **block** $b$ — a group of consecutive frames, say
$T_b = 0.5$ s $\approx 15$ frames — its own amplitude:

$$
P_{ik}(b) \;=\; \bar P_{ik}\, 10^{d_{ik}(b)/10} .
$$

Within the block the model is constant, so the block's cells around line
$(i,k)$ have density $S \propto P_{ik}(b)$ and, by (W1), the Whittle
likelihood of *those cells alone* pins $d_{ik}(b)$ to within
$4.34/\sqrt{n_{ik}(b)}$ dB, where $n_{ik}(b)$ is the number of cells the line
occupies in the block (its frames times the bins it spans). The likelihood
is not "blind" to the block amplitude; it is exactly as informative as the
count of cells allows.

What ties the blocks together is a **prior on the latents**, and that is
where $\sigma_d$ and the wander's memory $\tau_d$ live:

$$
d_{ik}(b+1) \;=\; \rho\, d_{ik}(b) + \sqrt{1-\rho^2}\,\sigma_d\,\varepsilon_b,
\qquad \rho = e^{-T_b/\tau_d},\quad \varepsilon_b \sim \mathcal N(0,1),
$$

an Ornstein–Uhlenbeck process sampled at the block rate: stationary sd
$\sigma_d$ (in dB), correlation time $\tau_d$. This is the same object as the shaft
OU of the phase model and the same object as the floor spline's Gaussian
prior — a smooth random curve with a known covariance — only now the
curve runs over blocks instead of over frequency control points.

**The information flow, in words.** Each block's cells say "my amplitude is
about this, $\pm$ a few dB". The prior says "consecutive blocks differ by
about $\sigma_d\sqrt{2(1-\rho)}$ dB, and all of them hover around the clip's
$\bar P_{ik}$". Combining the two gives (a) a smoothed amplitude track per
line, (b) an estimate of $\bar P_{ik}$ that is *less* biased than the
constant model's, and (c), from the spread and the lag-1 correlation of the
smoothed tracks, the wander parameters $\sigma_d, \tau_d$. Point (c) is what
the legacy model's `harm_gp_std_db` / `harm_gp_tau_s` sliders set by hand
and what v2 lost.

Nothing in this argument is specific to the comb: the floor's 14 spline
control values $c_j$ can carry a block latent $u_j(b)$ in exactly the same
way, which gives the floor level and colour their slow drift back
(the legacy `floor_gp_std_db`, `floor_color_*`).

## 1.5 Where the Whittle likelihood genuinely stops

The block construction removes the blindness, not every limitation. Four
remain and each is a design constraint on the block length and on what is
asked of the fit.

1. **Wander faster than a block is width.** A line whose power changes
   *within* a block is, to that block's periodogram, a broadened line. The
   block must be short against $\tau_d$; the measured order-tracked
   line-power autocorrelation (R4's estimator on real windows) decides
   $T_b$. If the real wander has a fast component, it stays in $\gamma$ —
   and then $\gamma$ is a physical width plus a modulation width, which the
   paper must say.
2. **Few cells, weak line: the latent is prior-dominated.** A line 3 dB over
   the floor spanning 3 bins in a 15-frame block has $n \approx 45$ cells
   but most of their power is floor; the effective count is far smaller.
   The posterior of $d_{ik}(b)$ then follows the prior — the fit will
   report "no evidence of wander" for such lines, not "no wander". Report
   $\sigma_d$ only from orders whose block-level sd is under, say, 2 dB
   (the slider in §1.6 shows the trade).
3. **A moving carrier inside the block smears the line.** The block
   periodogram is computed at fixed frequencies; if the rotor speed moves
   by $\delta$ rev/s across the block, order $k$ moves $k\delta$ Hz and the
   line's power spreads over bins. At 7.8 Hz per bin and a DREGON ramp of
   10 rev/s per second, a 0.5 s block moves order 10 by 50 Hz — six bins.
   Either the block periodogram is **carrier-aligned** (demodulate each
   frame at its own carrier before averaging, the order-domain instrument
   already in `tracking.order_domain`) or blocks are restricted to
   near-constant-speed spans. This is the same label-precision limit that
   set `k_max(T)` in the v2 plan.
4. **Rotors unresolved at low orders are one amplitude, not four.** At
   2048-point frames the four DREGON rotors' $k \le 8$ lines fall in the
   same bins. A per-rotor $d_{ik}(b)$ at those orders is not identifiable;
   only the rotor-sum's block amplitude is. Either share the low-order
   latent across rotors (as `flight_floor_lowk` shared the gain) or fit
   those orders on longer frames.

Beyond these, Whittle keeps its known structural blind spot: it uses the
**magnitude** of each cell and discards the cross-spectrum between
microphones and the phase relation between orders. Amplitude wander is a
magnitude effect, so this does not affect it; it affects the coherence
questions the R3 hump study raised and needs the cross-spectral Whittle
extension if they are ever pursued.

## 1.6 How much wander can a block resolve?

```{ojs}
viewof Tb = Inputs.range([0.1, 4], {value: 0.5, step: 0.1, label: "block length T_b (s)"})
viewof bins = Inputs.range([1, 9], {value: 3, step: 1, label: "bins a line occupies"})
viewof snr = Inputs.range([0, 30], {value: 6, step: 1, label: "line-to-floor ratio at the peak (dB)"})
viewof tauw = Inputs.range([0.5, 20], {value: 3, step: 0.5, label: "wander correlation time tau_w (s)"})
```

```{ojs}
frames = Math.max(1, Math.round(Tb * 16000 / 512))
cells = frames * bins
snrLin = Math.pow(10, snr / 10)
// fraction of a cell's power that belongs to the line, at the peak bin
lineFrac = snrLin / (1 + snrLin)
// effective cells: each cell informs the line scale with weight lineFrac^2 (delta-method)
nEff = cells * lineFrac * lineFrac
sdDb = 4.34 / Math.sqrt(nEff)
rho = Math.exp(-Tb / tauw)
html`<table>
<tr><td>frames per block</td><td>${frames}</td></tr>
<tr><td>cells per line per block</td><td>${cells}</td></tr>
<tr><td>effective cells (floor-diluted)</td><td>${nEff.toFixed(1)}</td></tr>
<tr><td><b>sd of one block's amplitude estimate</b></td><td><b>${sdDb.toFixed(2)} dB</b></td></tr>
<tr><td>block-to-block prior correlation ρ = e^(−T_b/τ_w)</td><td>${rho.toFixed(3)}</td></tr>
<tr><td>smallest wander sd the block can distinguish from noise (≈ sd/√2)</td><td>${(sdDb / Math.SQRT2).toFixed(2)} dB</td></tr>
</table>`
```

Reading: a 6 dB line over three bins in half-second blocks is measured to
about $\pm 1.1$ dB per block, so a wander of $\sigma_d \ge 1$ dB is
resolvable on it; a 0 dB line is not (sd $\pm 3$ dB). Longer blocks buy
precision at the cost of smearing (constraint 1 and 3). The legacy model
drew `harm_gp_std_db` in the 2–6 dB range, which is comfortably above the
threshold on any visible order.

# Part 2 — the modified model

Everything the review agreed, collected. Notation as on the supervisor deck:
mic $m$, rotor $i$ (or $r$), order $k$, block $b$, time $t$. Changes to v2
are marked **[new]**; the rest is v2 unchanged.

## 2.1 The signal

$$
x_m(t) \;=\; \sum_i\sum_k A_{mik}(t)\cos\phi_{ik}(t) \;+\; n_m(t) .
$$

One cosine per (rotor, order), plus broadband noise.

## 2.2 Phase

$$
\phi_{ik}(t) = 2\pi k\!\int_0^t f_i(s)\,ds \;+\; k\,\theta_i(t) \;+\; \psi_{ik}(t) \;+\; \alpha_{ik}
$$

- $f_i(t)$: the rotor's labelled speed (rev/s); given, from telemetry or the
  refined track.
- $\theta_i(t)$: the shaft's integrated speed error, one per rotor, shared by
  all its orders (multiplied by $k$):
  $d\nu_i = -\lambda\nu_i\,dt + \sqrt{2\lambda}\,\sigma_\nu\,dW_i,\;
  d\theta_i = \nu_i\,dt$. The $\sqrt{2\lambda}$ makes $\sigma_\nu$ the
  stationary sd of the speed error in rad/s, independent of $\lambda$ — the
  size and the memory are separate knobs.
- $\psi_{ik}(t)$: a per-line Wiener phase, increments $\mathcal N(0,
  4\pi\gamma_{ik}|\tau|)$, which makes the line a Lorentzian of half-width
  $\gamma_{ik}$ Hz (derivation: $\mathbb E[e^{i\Delta\psi}] = e^{-2\pi\gamma|\tau|}$,
  an exponential autocorrelation, whose transform is a Lorentzian of HWHM
  $\gamma$).
- $\alpha_{ik}$: a fixed random start phase.

**[new] priors.** $\sigma_\nu \sim$ HalfNormal$(s_\nu)$ in rad/s and
$\gamma_{ik}/(\gamma_0 k) \sim$ HalfNormal$(c_\gamma)$, with $\gamma_0 =
0.01$ Hz (the bench decoherence law) and $c_\gamma$ of order 3. Both are
light-tailed in **linear** units: a width of $5\gamma_0 k$ costs 1.4 nats,
$13$ Hz at $k=1$ costs $\sim 10^5$ nats. No truncation — the penalty is
smooth everywhere, so L-BFGS in the unconstrained space never stalls at a
wall — but nothing the data does not demand can be wide. The current
LogNormal$(\log 0.01k,\;1.0)$ is removed.

## 2.3 Line amplitude

$$
A_{mik}(t) \;=\; \sqrt{2}\;
10^{\,\big(p_{ik} \;+\; d_{ik}(b(t))\;+\; 10a\log_{10}\frac{f_i(t)}{f_{\mathrm{ref}}}\big)/20}\;
10^{\,e_{mi}/20}
$$

Everything multiplicative in power is additive in decibels, and the fit
works in decibels, so every level is written as $10^{(\cdot)/10}$ on power
and $10^{(\cdot)/20}$ on amplitude (the square root). Term by term:

- $p_{ik}$: the line's **mean** power in dB at the reference speed
  $f_{\mathrm{ref}} = 80$ rev/s (`profile_db`, unchanged).
- $10a\log_{10}(f_i/f_{\mathrm{ref}})$: the speed law, $a$ = `amp_exp`,
  prior $\mathcal N(2, 1)$, pinned at 2 when the pool's speed span is under
  1.5× (unchanged).
- **[new]** $d_{ik}(b)$: the block wander of §1.4, **in dB** (not nepers —
  the same unit as every other level, so a fitted $\sigma_d = 3$ reads as
  "3 dB"). Hierarchical: $d_{ik}(b) = d_i(b) + v_{ik}(b)$, a per-rotor
  common part (all orders of a rotor breathe together — the legacy
  `harm_coherence` at 1) plus a per-line residual, each an OU across blocks
  with its own $(\sigma, \tau)$: $(\sigma_d, \tau_d)$ and
  $(\sigma_v, \tau_v)$. Priors on the four hyperparameters: HalfNormal on the
  sds with scale from the R4 order-tracked line-power spread on real
  windows; LogNormal on the times centred on the measured autocorrelation
  time.
- **[new]** $e_{mi}$: the microphone term, see §2.5. On the evidence of the
  rank test it is expected to be **zero** once channels are normalised; the
  model keeps at most one free directivity offset per rotor,
  $e_{mi} = \delta_i$ with $\delta_i \sim \mathcal N(0, 3)$ dB, to be
  introduced only if the residuals ask for it.

**[new] one prior for every order — no visibility switch.** v2 decides
*before the fit* whether an order is "visible" (measured excess $\ge 2$ dB
over the floor on the pooled periodogram → $\mathcal N(\text{measured},
10)$) or not (→ parked at $\mathcal N(\text{floor} - 15, 8)$). That switch
was a patch: in R1, invisible orders parked at a flat $\mathcal N(-45, 40)$
*with free widths* summed into a 400 Hz pedestal over the floor. With the
half-normal width prior of §2.2 a line is a needle covering one to three
bins, and needles cannot build a pedestal — to raise the level between
orders the model would have to raise the floor, and the Whittle term at the
bins with no line forbids that. So an order without evidence has exactly
one thing it can do: **sink**. The likelihood pushes it down until its
contribution at its own bins is negligible (about 10 dB under the floor,
where it adds 0.4 dB), and below that the likelihood is flat. Nothing has
to be decided in advance, and the prior only has to be wide enough not to
get in the way:

$$
p_{ik} \;\sim\; \mathcal N\big(\hat p_{ik},\; 10\ \mathrm{dB}\big)
\quad\text{for every } (i, k),
$$

with $\hat p_{ik}$ the pooled periodogram level at $k f_i$ — line plus
floor, i.e. an upper bound on the line. Sinking 20 dB below it costs 2 nats,
nothing against the Whittle sum; rising above it is priced by the likelihood
itself (over-predicting a bin costs linearly in $S/I$), so no upper-side
prior is needed. `Measured.profile_prior` becomes one line;
`line_visible_snr_db`, `profile_below_offset_db`, `profile_below_sd` go.

Two things this deliberately does **not** do. It adds no trend across orders
(the legacy "gain + slope × log k" prior): that would make the model
extrapolate a comb where the data is silent, and on DREGON free flight it
would hold a line that the label puts in the wrong bin up at the wrong
frequency. And it does not rescue label-displaced lines: an order whose
label frequency is off by more than a bin has genuinely no power at the
label frequency and *will* sink — the correct fit of a wrong label. The fix
for that is the per-rotor carrier deviation track (Part 4), not a prior.

## 2.4 The floor

$$
S_m(f, t) \;=\;
\Big[\tfrac1R\textstyle\sum_i \big(\tfrac{f_i(t)}{f_{\mathrm{ref}}}\big)^{b} + s\Big]\;
10^{\,C(f,\,b(t))/10}
\;+\; W_m(f)
$$

- The bracket is unchanged: the rotor-mean speed law with exponent $b$
  (`floor_exp`, LN$(\log 2, 0.5)$, pinned on short spans) plus the static
  fraction $s$ (`floor_static_rel`).
- **[new]** $C(f, b)$: the floor shape in dB is **the spline alone**,
  $C(f,b) = \sum_{j=1}^{14} B_j(f)\,c_j(b)$, with $B_j$ the linear
  interpolation weights on the geometric control grid 30 … 8000 Hz. The
  separate mean $\mu_F$ and tilt $t_F$ are dropped: on this grid the spline
  already spans a constant and a straight line in $\log f$, so the three
  were collinear and the fits split them arbitrarily
  (`michaels_fly125_cruise__flight.json`: tilt $-0.04$ dB/oct, spline
  swing $+19 \to -58$ dB, $\|z\| = 13.9$ against a prior expectation of
  $\sqrt{14} = 3.7$; `dregon_room2_floor__flight_profile.json`: tilt
  $-5.6$ dB/oct and a $+8$ dB spline bump — same total, different split).
  The control values are $c_j(b) = \bar c_j + u_j(b)$:
  - $\bar c_j = \mu + \sigma_B (L z)_j$, $z \sim \mathcal N(0, I)$, $L$ the
    Cholesky factor of the squared-exponential kernel across control points
    (as now), $\mu$ the measured band median, and $\sigma_B$ **measured**
    from the real windows' floor-shape spread rather than a constant — so
    the $z$ prior binds. If the fits still run off, the same light-tailed
    penalty as for $\gamma$ applies to $z$.
  - **[new]** $u_j(b)$, in dB: the floor's slow drift, an OU across blocks
    shared by all control points for the level (one latent $u(b)$) plus a
    per-control-point residual for the colour — the same two-level
    structure as the comb wander, with its own $(\sigma_u, \tau_u)$.
- **[new]** $W_m(f)$: a per-microphone **static** low-frequency term for
  wind / capsule self-noise: a fixed shape concentrated below ~500 Hz with
  one free level per mic, not scaled by rotor speed and not scaled by the
  channel gain (wind noise is generated at the capsule, so it is genuinely
  per channel and uncorrelated with the acoustic field). Present for
  DREGON only — see the measurement in §2.5. There is **no** per-mic gain on
  the shared floor.

## 2.5 Microphones: what the real windows say

The v2 fit carries three per-mic blocks — `mic_gains_db` (everything at mic
$m$), `mic_line_gain_db` (rotor $i$'s comb at mic $m$), `mic_floor_db` (the
floor at mic $m$), all mean-centred, all $\mathcal N(0, 6)$: 48 numbers for
16 observable sums, split by the priors alone. The rank test
(`results/noise_v2/mic_gains/findings.md`, commit `276f29e0`; DREGON 50
windows over six nosource flights plus 20 bench windows, Michael's 11
windows; per-window 1/3-octave levels, comb cells and floor cells separated)
asked whether the per-mic deviation is one gain per channel:

| | Michael's | DREGON, all bands | DREGON, bands ≥ 500 Hz | DREGON, ≥ 1 kHz |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| one gain per mic explains (floor) | 75.7 %, residual 1.62 dB | 35.9 %, 3.35 dB | 37 %, 1.76 dB | 67 %, 1.00 dB |
| one gain per mic **per band** | 93.1 %, 0.87 dB | 73.8 %, 2.14 dB | | < 1 dB |
| corr(comb gains, floor gains) | **0.996** (RMS diff 0.35 dB) | 0.846 (1.37 dB) | **0.990** (0.19 dB) | **1.000** (0.05 dB) |
| gain span across mics | 9.8 dB | | ±2.3 dB | |
| per-mic floor excess, < 500 Hz vs > 500 Hz | 2.4 vs 3.7 dB (not low-frequency) | **4.9 vs 1.4 dB** (low-frequency, ±6 dB per channel) | | |
| excess vs rotor speed | 1.1 dB/oct over 1.27 oct (none) | flight span 0.07 oct: unidentifiable; bench 0.85 oct: ≤ 3 dB/oct, 0/8 significant | | |

What it means, rig by rig:

- **Michael's.** Comb and floor share one per-channel gain to 0.35 dB; the
  gains span 10 dB. That is channel *sensitivity*: some capsules recorded
  the same sound louder. It belongs in the data pipeline, not in the model
  — normalise the eight channels once by their measured gains and drop all
  three mic blocks. The remaining 1.6 dB is a mild per-channel frequency
  response in 3–8 kHz; a fixed per-channel per-band equalisation (93 %)
  is available if ever wanted, again as calibration rather than parameter.
- **DREGON.** Above 500 Hz it is the same picture (correlation 0.99, gains
  within 0.2 dB between comb and floor); the whole "comb and floor
  disagree" verdict of the all-band test was the sub-500 Hz excess. That
  excess is ±6 dB per channel, low-frequency, and on the bench (the only
  DREGON data with a speed span) does not follow rotor speed: wind /
  self-noise, per capsule. So DREGON gets the same one-per-channel
  normalisation, measured on bands ≥ 500 Hz, plus the static per-mic term
  $W_m(f)$ below 500 Hz. Its no-speed-scaling is backed by the bench, not
  by flight (the flight windows span 78.7–82.4 rev/s and can never separate
  "speed-scaled" from "static").

And the rotor→microphone geometry term that the review first proposed for
the comb ($-20\log_{10} d_{mi}/d_{\mathrm{ref}}$): after the common
sensitivity is removed, the comb-minus-floor gain differences are 0.05–0.3
dB on both rigs, so on this evidence there is nothing left for a geometry
term to explain. The model starts **without** it; a per-rotor directivity
offset $\delta_i$ is the fallback if the residuals of the refit disagree.

## 2.6 What is fitted where

| quantity | per | prior / status |
|---|---|---|
| $p_{ik}$ | rig | $\mathcal N(\hat p_{ik}, 10\ \mathrm{dB})$ for every order; no visibility switch **[new]** |
| $\gamma_{ik}$ | rig | HalfNormal in linear units, scale $c_\gamma \gamma_0 k$ **[new]** |
| $\sigma_\nu$ | rig | HalfNormal **[new]**; $\lambda$ pinned in flight (unchanged) |
| $a$, $b$, $s$ | rig | unchanged; pinned on short-span pools |
| $\bar c_j$ via $z$, $\mu$ | rig | $\mathcal N(0, I)$ with measured $\sigma_B$; $\mu_F$, $t_F$ removed **[new]** |
| channel gains | data | normalised once per rig from the rank test (bands ≥ 500 Hz); no mic blocks in the fit **[new]** |
| $W_m$ level | rig (per mic) | DREGON only, static, < 500 Hz **[new]** |
| $\delta_i$ | rig | not in the first fit; $\mathcal N(0, 3)$ dB fallback **[new]** |
| $d_i(b)$, $v_{ik}(b)$, $u(b)$, $u_j(b)$ | clip × block | OU latents in dB **[new]** |
| $\sigma_d, \tau_d, \sigma_v, \tau_v, \sigma_u, \tau_u$ | rig | HalfNormal / LogNormal, centred on measured statistics **[new]** |

# Part 3 — fitting, line by line

## 3.1 Data

1. Windows of real audio with a rotor-speed label: the same supports as v2
   (`experiments.noise_model.supports`), 8 microphones, 16 kHz.
2. Each window → frames ($N = 2048$, hop 512, periodic Hann) → periodogram
   cells $I_m(n, f)$, one per (mic, frame, bin), in the units the forward
   model uses (`spectrum.py`'s work-grid convention). Bins in the fit band
   30 – 7900 Hz.
3. **[new]** Frames are grouped into blocks of $T_b$ seconds. $T_b$ is not a
   free parameter: it is set from the measured autocorrelation time of
   order-tracked line power on real windows (R4's estimator) at roughly
   $\tau_d/4$, and checked against constraint 3 of §1.5 (carrier motion
   inside a block under one bin at the highest fitted order; blocks that
   violate it are dropped or carrier-aligned).
4. Per frame, the carriers $f_i(n)$ from the label; per block, the
   block-mean carriers and the speed factors.

## 3.2 The forward model of a block

For block $b$ of a window, the model predicts the density at every (mic,
bin):

$$
S_m(b, f) \;=\; \sum_i \sum_k P_{ik}(b)\,10^{g_{mi}/10}\;\mathcal L_{ik}\big(f - k\bar f_i(b)\big)
\;+\; S^{\text{floor}}_m(b, f)
$$

- $P_{ik}(b) = \bar P_{ik}\,(\bar f_i(b)/f_{\mathrm{ref}})^{a}\,10^{d_{ik}(b)/10}$, with $g_{mi}$ now the fixed channel normalisation (zero after the data is normalised) plus $W_m$ in the floor.
- $\mathcal L_{ik}$ is the line shape: the Lorentzian of half-width
  $\gamma_{ik}$ convolved with the shaft's Gaussian core of sd
  $k\sigma_\nu/2\pi$ Hz and with the frame window's transform — exactly the
  R3 line-shape kernel `spectrum.py` evaluates now, unchanged.
- $S^{\text{floor}}_m(b, f)$ is §2.4 with $C(f, b)$ at the block's control
  values and the block-mean speed factor.

This is the current `flight_model` with two extra inputs per block, the
latent vectors $w(b)$ and $u(b)$. Nothing else in the forward model changes.

## 3.3 The objective

$$
\mathcal J \;=\; \underbrace{\sum_{\text{windows}}\sum_{m,b,n\in b,f}\Big[\log S_m(b,f) + \tfrac{I_m(n,f)}{S_m(b,f)}\Big]}_{\text{Whittle, per block}}
\;+\; \underbrace{\sum_{\text{latents}} \tfrac12\, \mathbf d^\top \Sigma_{\text{OU}}^{-1}\mathbf d}_{\text{block priors}}
\;+\; \underbrace{\sum_{\text{rig params}} -\log \pi(\theta)}_{\text{rig priors}}
$$

Line by line:

1. **Whittle per block.** Every frame $n$ inside block $b$ is compared to
   the block's density $S_m(b, f)$. The frames of a block share the latent,
   the blocks of a window share the rig parameters, the windows of a rig
   share everything but the latents.
2. **Block priors.** For each latent track (one per rotor for $d_i$, one per
   line for $v_{ik}$, one for $u$, one per control point for $u_j$), the OU
   quadratic form: with $\rho = e^{-T_b/\tau}$ and $B$ blocks,
   $\tfrac12\big[d_1^2/\sigma^2 + \sum_{b\ge 2}(d_b - \rho d_{b-1})^2/(\sigma^2(1-\rho^2))\big]
   + \tfrac{B}{2}\log\sigma^2 + \tfrac{B-1}{2}\log(1-\rho^2)$.
   The two log terms are what let $\sigma$ and $\tau$ be fitted at all: a
   small $\sigma$ makes the quadratic cheap but the $\log\sigma^2$ term
   expensive, and the optimum sits where the latents' actual spread equals
   $\sigma$.
3. **Rig priors.** The list of §2.6, each as $-\log$ density in the
   unconstrained parametrisation Pyro uses (HalfNormal via a softplus /
   absolute-value bijector, LogNormal via $\log$).

::: {.callout-warning}
## The one place joint MAP is known to cheat

Maximising $\mathcal J$ jointly over the latents **and** their variance
hyperparameters $\sigma_d, \sigma_v, \sigma_u$ underestimates the variances:
the latents shrink toward zero and the hyperparameter follows them. The
section below derives it on the smallest example that has the problem, then
derives the cure — integrating the latents out — first exactly for the
Gaussian toy, then as the Laplace approximation the real objective needs.
:::

## 3.3a Why joint MAP cheats, and the marginal likelihood that does not

### The toy

Keep one line and forget the OU memory. There are $B$ blocks; block $b$ has
a latent amplitude offset $d_b$ (dB) drawn from the wander distribution, and
the block's Whittle term, expanded around its optimum, is a Gaussian
measurement of that offset:

$$
d_b \sim \mathcal N(0, \sigma^2), \qquad
y_b \,|\, d_b \sim \mathcal N(d_b,\, s^2),
$$

where $y_b$ is the block's own amplitude estimate (the MLE of the block
scale from its cells) and $s$ its standard error — the $4.34/\sqrt{n_{\rm eff}}$
dB of §1.6, **known**, set by the cell count. The unknowns are the $B$
latents $d_1..d_B$ and the one hyperparameter $\sigma$. (The real objective
has an OU prior instead of independent $\mathcal N(0,\sigma^2)$ and a
non-Gaussian Whittle term instead of $\mathcal N(d_b, s^2)$; neither changes
the mechanism, and §"Laplace" below puts them back.)

### Joint MAP

The negative log joint density of everything, dropping constants:

$$
\mathcal J(d, \sigma) \;=\; \underbrace{\sum_b \frac{(y_b - d_b)^2}{2 s^2}}_{\text{likelihood}}
\;+\; \underbrace{\sum_b \frac{d_b^2}{2\sigma^2} + B\log\sigma}_{\text{prior of the latents}} .
$$

The $B\log\sigma$ is the normalising constant of the $B$ Gaussian priors,
$\tfrac12\log(2\pi\sigma^2)$ each; it is what stops $\sigma$ from being
driven to infinity (where the quadratic term vanishes). Now minimise.

**Over the latents, at fixed $\sigma$.** $\partial\mathcal J/\partial d_b = 0$:

$$
-\frac{y_b - d_b}{s^2} + \frac{d_b}{\sigma^2} = 0
\;\;\Rightarrow\;\;
\hat d_b \;=\; \frac{\sigma^2}{\sigma^2 + s^2}\; y_b \;=:\; \kappa\, y_b .
$$

The estimate is the measurement **shrunk** toward the prior mean by the
factor $\kappa \in (0,1)$: when the block is precise ($s \ll \sigma$) it is
trusted, when it is noisy the prior wins. Correct and standard.

**Over $\sigma$, at fixed latents.** $\partial\mathcal J/\partial\sigma = 0$:

$$
-\frac{\sum_b d_b^2}{\sigma^3} + \frac{B}{\sigma} = 0
\;\;\Rightarrow\;\;
\hat\sigma^2 \;=\; \frac1B\sum_b d_b^2 .
$$

The variance estimate is the sample variance of the latents. Also correct
**if the latents were the truth**. But they are not: they are the shrunk
estimates. Substitute:

$$
\hat\sigma^2 \;=\; \kappa^2\;\overline{y^2},
\qquad \kappa = \frac{\hat\sigma^2}{\hat\sigma^2 + s^2} .
$$

This is a fixed-point equation in $\hat\sigma^2$. Write $v = \hat\sigma^2$
and $m = \overline{y^2}$ (the observed spread of the block estimates, which
in truth equals $\sigma^2 + s^2$):

$$
v \;=\; \Big(\frac{v}{v + s^2}\Big)^{2} m
\;\;\Rightarrow\;\;
v = 0 \quad\text{or}\quad (v + s^2)^2 = v\, m
\;\;\Rightarrow\;\;
v \;=\; \frac{m - 2s^2 \pm \sqrt{m(m - 4s^2)}}{2} .
$$

Read it: (i) $v = 0$ — "no wander at all" — is **always** a solution,
whatever the data; (ii) a positive solution exists only if $m > 4s^2$, i.e.
if the observed spread is more than **twice** the measurement noise
(in sd); (iii) even then, the larger root is below the honest value
$m - s^2$ (check with $s \to 0$: $v \to m$, fine; with $m = 5s^2$: honest
$v = 4s^2$, joint MAP $v = (3 + \sqrt5)/2\, s^2 \approx 2.6\, s^2$ — a 35 %
underestimate of the variance, and the small root is 0.4 $s^2$).
Iterating the two steps from any start converges to one of these; with
noisy blocks, to zero. That is the cheat: $B$ latents and one variance,
each latent shrunk by a factor that depends on the variance, and the
variance estimated from the shrunk latents. It is the same reason the MLE of
a Gaussian's variance divides by $n$ rather than $n-1$, compounded $B$
times.

### The marginal likelihood

The mistake was to treat the latents as parameters to be *optimised*. They
are random effects: what we actually want is the probability of the data
**averaged over everything the latents could have been**, as a function of
$\sigma$ alone,

$$
p(y \,|\, \sigma) \;=\; \prod_b \int p(y_b \,|\, d_b)\, p(d_b \,|\, \sigma)\, \mathrm d d_b .
$$

For the toy the integral is a textbook Gaussian convolution: a Gaussian
measurement of a Gaussian variable is a Gaussian with the variances added,

$$
\int \mathcal N(y_b;\, d_b, s^2)\;\mathcal N(d_b;\, 0, \sigma^2)\; \mathrm d d_b
\;=\; \mathcal N(y_b;\; 0,\; \sigma^2 + s^2).
$$

(To see it without a table: the exponent is
$-\tfrac{(y-d)^2}{2s^2} - \tfrac{d^2}{2\sigma^2}$, a quadratic in $d$;
complete the square in $d$, integrate the Gaussian in $d$ — which gives a
factor $\sqrt{2\pi\,\sigma^2 s^2/(\sigma^2+s^2)}$ — and what is left in $y$
is $-\tfrac{y^2}{2(\sigma^2+s^2)}$.) So the negative log marginal is

$$
\mathcal M(\sigma) \;=\; \sum_b \Big[\frac{y_b^2}{2(\sigma^2 + s^2)} + \tfrac12\log(\sigma^2 + s^2)\Big],
\qquad
\frac{\partial\mathcal M}{\partial\sigma^2} = 0
\;\Rightarrow\;
\hat\sigma^2 \;=\; \overline{y^2} - s^2 .
$$

**Observed spread minus measurement noise** — the honest answer, no
shrinkage loop, $v = 0$ is no longer a spurious solution. Compare the two
objectives term by term: the marginal has $\log(\sigma^2 + s^2)$ where the
joint had $\log\sigma^2$ *and* it has no latents to shrink; the
$s^2$ inside the log is exactly the block-level uncertainty that the joint
objective threw away when it replaced "average over $d_b$" by "plug in the
best $d_b$".

**Moment matching is the same formula from the other side.** After a joint
fit at some $\sigma$, the posterior of $d_b$ given $y_b$ is Gaussian with
mean $\kappa y_b$ and variance $\sigma^2 s^2/(\sigma^2 + s^2)$ (complete the
square again). Then
$\mathbb E[d_b^2 \,|\, y] = (\kappa y_b)^2 + \sigma^2 s^2/(\sigma^2+s^2)$, and
the EM update of the variance, $\hat\sigma^2 = \tfrac1B\sum_b \mathbb E[d_b^2\,|\,y]$,
is "sample variance of the shrunk latents **plus** their posterior
variance" — the moment-matching recipe of the box. Iterating it converges
to the marginal maximiser $\overline{y^2} - s^2$; that is why the two
remedies agree, and why the first is just the second done by hand.

### Method of moments: no Laplace, no posterior

The marginal result $\hat\sigma^2 = \overline{y^2} - s^2$ can be reached
without integrating anything, by asking only what the **first two moments**
of the block estimates must be under the model. This route needs no
Gaussian approximation of the Whittle term, because it never uses the
likelihood's *shape* — only the sampling distribution of one number per
block, which the Whittle model gives exactly.

**Step 1 — what a block estimate is.** With the rig parameters held fixed
(from the fit without latents, step (i) of §3.4), block $b$ of line $(i,k)$
has one unknown, its amplitude offset $d_b$, and its Whittle term
$W_b(d_b)$ is maximised by the block's scale estimate — call it $y_b$. In
the pure-line case (cells dominated by the line) $y_b$ is $10\log_{10}$ of
the mean of $n$ exponential cells divided by their model mean, i.e.

$$
10^{y_b/10} \;=\; 10^{d_b/10}\;\cdot\; \frac{1}{n}\sum_{c=1}^{n} E_c,
\qquad E_c \sim \mathrm{Exp}(1) \text{ i.i.d.},
$$

so $y_b = d_b + \epsilon_b$ with $\epsilon_b = 10\log_{10}\big(\tfrac1n\sum E_c\big)$
— a **known** distribution: $\tfrac1n\sum E_c \sim \mathrm{Gamma}(n, 1/n)$,
and for its log the mean and variance are exact,

$$
\mathbb E[\epsilon_b] = \tfrac{10}{\ln 10}\big(\psi(n) - \ln n\big) \approx -\tfrac{2.17}{n}\ \mathrm{dB},
\qquad
\operatorname{Var}[\epsilon_b] = \big(\tfrac{10}{\ln 10}\big)^2 \psi_1(n) \approx \frac{18.9}{n}\ \mathrm{dB}^2
= \Big(\frac{4.34}{\sqrt n}\Big)^2,
$$

with $\psi, \psi_1$ the digamma and trigamma functions. This is the
$s^2$ of the toy, exact rather than asymptotic, and it depends on nothing
but the cell count. (For a line over a floor, $n$ becomes the effective
count of §1.6; if one does not trust the delta-method version of that, the
variance of $\epsilon_b$ is obtained by **simulation under the model** —
draw cells from the model's own density with $d_b = 0$, compute $y_b$,
repeat — which is exact to Monte-Carlo error and still involves no
approximation of the likelihood.) Independence across blocks holds because
the cells of different blocks are disjoint, and $\epsilon_b$ is independent
of $d_b$ because the cells' randomness is the exponential law, not the
wander.

**Step 2 — the moment equations.** Now $y_b = d_b + \epsilon_b$ with
$d_b$ the OU latent (mean 0, variance $\sigma^2$, lag-$l$ covariance
$\sigma^2\rho^{l}$) and $\epsilon_b$ the measurement error (mean $\mu_\epsilon$,
variance $s^2$, independent across blocks and of $d$). Taking expectations:

$$
\mathbb E[y_b] = \mu_\epsilon, \qquad
\operatorname{Var}[y_b] = \sigma^2 + s^2, \qquad
\operatorname{Cov}[y_b, y_{b+l}] = \sigma^2 \rho^{l}\quad (l \ge 1).
$$

The measurement error appears **only** in the variance, never in the
covariances — noise in different blocks is independent. Replace the
population moments by their sample versions over the $B$ blocks (and over
windows, and over the lines that share the hyperparameter) and solve:

$$
\hat\sigma^2 \;=\; \widehat{\operatorname{Var}}[y] - s^2,
\qquad
\hat\rho \;=\; \frac{\widehat{\operatorname{Cov}}_1[y]}{\hat\sigma^2}
\;\;\Rightarrow\;\;
\hat\tau = -\,T_b / \ln\hat\rho .
$$

The first is the marginal-likelihood answer of the previous section,
obtained with no integral; the second is the Yule–Walker estimate of an
AR(1) observed through noise, and it gives $\tau$ **as well** — the lag-1
covariance is untouched by the measurement noise, so $\tau$ needs no
correction at all. (A more robust variant uses several lags,
$\widehat{\operatorname{Cov}}_l = \sigma^2\rho^l$, and fits $\log$-linearly
in $l$; with $B = 16$ blocks per window and hundreds of windows, lags 1–4
are well populated.)

**Step 3 — the hierarchical split, also by moments.** The comb wander was
written $d_{ik}(b) = d_i(b) + v_{ik}(b)$, a per-rotor common part and a
per-line residual. Two lines $k \ne k'$ of the same rotor in the same block
share $d_i(b)$ and have independent $v$ and independent $\epsilon$, so

$$
\operatorname{Cov}[y_{ik}(b),\, y_{ik'}(b)] = \sigma_d^2,
\qquad
\operatorname{Var}[y_{ik}(b)] = \sigma_d^2 + \sigma_v^2 + s_{ik}^2 .
$$

The **cross-order covariance** at one block is the common variance
directly; the residual variance follows by subtraction. The legacy model's
`harm_coherence` was exactly this ratio $\sigma_d^2/(\sigma_d^2+\sigma_v^2)$,
set by hand; here it is a measured moment. The same construction on the
floor control points gives $\sigma_u$ (level: covariance across control
points) and the colour residual.

**Why this is honest, and what it costs.** Every equation above is an
identity of the model — no expansion, no Gaussian assumption on the
Whittle term, no posterior. The price is statistical efficiency: a method of
moments uses only second moments, so with few blocks its estimates are
noisier than maximum likelihood's, and $\widehat{\operatorname{Var}}[y] -
s^2$ can come out **negative** on a line whose wander is below its
measurement noise (constraint 2 of §1.5). That is not a defect to hide: it
means "no wander resolvable on this line", the estimate is clipped to zero
and the line is excluded from the pooled $\hat\sigma$, exactly as the
§1.6 threshold prescribes. Pool over orders with $s_{ik} < \sigma$-ish
(the resolvable ones) and over windows, and the estimates are as good as
the data allows.

**Relation to the earlier "moment matching".** The recipe first stated in
the box — variance of the shrunk MAP latents plus their posterior variance
— is the EM update and needs the posterior variance, which for a
non-Gaussian block term is itself a Laplace quantity ($1/h_b$). The version
here bypasses the joint fit altogether for the hyperparameters: it takes
the *unshrunk* block estimates $y_b$ and the *exact* noise variance $s_b^2$
and solves the moment equations. The joint fit is still what produces the
smoothed latent tracks for rendering and for the rig-parameter refit
(step (iii) of §3.4), but $\sigma$ and $\tau$ are not read off it.

### Laplace: the likelihood route, kept as the check

In the real fit two things are not Gaussian-exact: the block term is the
Whittle sum, not $\mathcal N(d_b, s^2)$, and the prior is an OU chain across
blocks, not independent. The OU prior is still Gaussian — with covariance
$\Sigma_{\rm OU}$ (entries $\sigma^2 \rho^{|b - b'|}$) — so the only
approximation needed is on the Whittle side. **Laplace's method** replaces
the block Whittle term by its second-order Taylor expansion around its
optimum $\hat d_b$:

$$
W_b(d_b) \;\approx\; W_b(\hat d_b) + \tfrac12\, h_b\, (d_b - \hat d_b)^2,
\qquad h_b = \frac{\partial^2 W_b}{\partial d_b^2}\Big|_{\hat d_b},
$$

which is exactly the toy's $\mathcal N(y_b, s^2)$ with $y_b = \hat d_b$ and
$s_b^2 = 1/h_b$ — the block's own Fisher information. Then the integral
over the latents is Gaussian again and the negative log marginal is

$$
\mathcal M(\sigma, \tau) \;=\; \sum_b W_b(\hat d_b)
\;+\; \tfrac12\,\hat{\mathbf d}^\top (\Sigma_{\rm OU} + H^{-1})^{-1}\hat{\mathbf d}
\;+\; \tfrac12 \log\det\big(\Sigma_{\rm OU} + H^{-1}\big) \;+\; \text{const},
$$

with $H = \operatorname{diag}(h_b)$. The toy is the case $\Sigma_{\rm OU} =
\sigma^2 I$, $H = I/s^2$. The recipe per window: (1) at the current
$(\sigma, \tau)$, find the MAP latents $\hat{\mathbf d}$ (this is step (ii)
of §3.4 — it has to be done anyway); (2) compute the block curvatures $h_b$
(one second derivative of the Whittle sum per block, cheap — it is a sum
over that block's cells of $I/S^2$-type terms); (3) evaluate $\mathcal M$
and its gradient in $(\sigma, \tau)$ and take a step; repeat. The
$\log\det$ is of a $B \times B$ matrix per latent track, $B \approx 16$ —
negligible. This is the standard mixed-model / INLA construction, and it is
what the "Laplace" remedy of the box means. Its error is the Whittle term's
deviation from a parabola in $d_b$ over the width of the posterior, which
for a log-scale parameter with $n_{\rm eff} \gtrsim 10$ cells is small.

**What to use.** The method of moments for the hyperparameters
$(\sigma_d, \tau_d, \sigma_v, \sigma_u, \ldots)$: it is exact under the
model, needs no posterior and no Laplace step, and yields $\tau$ for free
from the lag covariances. The joint fit then runs with those
hyperparameters fixed, producing the latent tracks and the refit of the rig
parameters; alternate the two until the moments stop moving. The Laplace
marginal stays as a *check* on the moment estimates where the blocks are
precise ($n_{\rm eff} \gtrsim 10$), not as the estimator.

## 3.4 The optimisation

1. **Parametrisation.** All rig parameters and all latents live in one
   unconstrained vector: Pyro sites as now (`sample_params`), with the
   latents as additional `to_event` sites inside a per-window plate. An
   8 s window at $T_b = 0.5$ s has 16 blocks; with $R = 4$, $K = 88$ that
   is $16\,(4 + 4\cdot 88 + 1 + 14) \approx 5\,900$ latents per window.
   L-BFGS handles that; what it cannot handle is a pool of 250 windows
   with all latents free at once, so:
2. **Alternation.** (i) With latents at zero, fit the rig parameters on the
   pool exactly as v2 does (warm start from the current fits — their
   profile and floor values are usable once re-expressed in the new
   parametrisation; the mic blocks are replaced by the data
   normalisation). (ii) With rig parameters fixed, fit each window's
   latents independently — the windows decouple, so this is 250 small
   L-BFGS problems, embarrassingly parallel on `uni-cpu`. (iii) Re-fit the
   rig parameters with the latents fixed. (iv) Re-estimate the
   hyperparameters by the method of moments on the block estimates
   (§3.3a). Repeat (ii)–(iv) until the Whittle term moves by
   less than the v2 tolerance ($10^{-4}$ nats/cell). Three to five rounds
   in practice for this kind of model; each round is one `uni-cpu` job.
3. **Restarts and pins** as v2: four seeds, the speed-law span pin, $\lambda$
   pinned in flight. The half-normal priors make the restarts far less
   necessary — the width degeneracy that produced the restart spread is
   gone — but they stay as the convergence check.
4. **Convergence label** on every fit as now (`which_converged`).

## 3.5 What to check before believing it

1. **Prior predictive.** Render the prior alone (no data) and confirm no
   line wider than a few $\gamma_0 k$ and no floor swing beyond the measured
   $\sigma_B$ appears — the priors now forbid the v2 pathologies by
   construction, and this is the test that they do.
2. **Held-out statistic.** The R4 order-tracked line-power spread across
   frames within a window, on real windows **not** in the pool, against the
   same statistic on renders from the fit. v2 cannot match it (it renders
   zero spread); the new fit's $\sigma_d, \sigma_v$ should.
3. **The tonality audit** (`results/noise_v2/rig_sampler/tonality/`) on the
   refitted rigs, now on rendered audio as well as on the expectation.
4. **The parity gate** unchanged (HPPNet on renders vs real), with the
   caveat already recorded that it measures familiarity, not transfer; the
   transfer test is a retrained arm.

# Part 4 — what this does not decide

- Whether the rotor-speed label needs its own per-rotor deviation track in
  DREGON free flight (the R5 follow-up). The block construction reduces the
  damage of label error (a block whose carrier is off just gets a wrong
  alignment for that block) but does not remove it; the carrier-aligned
  block periodogram of §1.5 (3) is the cheap mitigation.
- Cross-microphone coherence and inter-order phase relations: outside the
  Whittle magnitude likelihood, unchanged from v2.
- The trajectory model, the regime composition, the speed-law pins: all
  unchanged.

::: {.callout-note}
## Decisions taken in the review (2026-09-22), for the record

1. Half-normal, linear-space priors on $\gamma_{ik}$ and $\sigma_\nu$; no
   truncation.
2. No visibility switch: one prior $\mathcal N(\hat p_{ik}, 10\ \mathrm{dB})$ per
   order; with needle lines an order without evidence can only sink, which
   the likelihood does on its own. No trend prior across orders.
3. Slow amplitude wander restored: per-block OU latents **in dB** for line
   power (rotor-common + per-line) and for the floor spline (level + colour),
   with hyperparameters from the method of moments on the block estimates
   (§3.3a; Laplace marginal as the check).
4. Floor shape = spline only; $\mu_F$ and $t_F$ removed; $\sigma_B$ measured.
5. Channel gains: the rank test (`276f29e0`) holds on both rigs above
   500 Hz (comb–floor gain correlation 0.996 Michael's, 0.990 DREGON) →
   normalise the channels once per rig in the data, measured on bands
   ≥ 500 Hz; no mic blocks in the fit; no geometry term in the first fit
   (residual 0.05–0.3 dB); DREGON gets a per-mic static sub-500 Hz wind term.
6. The paper: state the $\sqrt{2\lambda}$ parametrisation's reason (σ_ν as
   the stationary sd) and the Wiener-phase → Lorentzian derivation (appendix).
7. No refit is started until authorised.
:::
